title: Strong vs. Weak Range Avoidance and the Linear Ordering Principle
authors: Oliver Korten (Columbia University, USA), Tonnian Pitassi (Columbia University, USA)
abstract: In a pair of recent breakthroughs it was shown that the classes S2E, ZPENP, and Sigma2E require exponential circuit complexity, giving the first unconditional improvements to a classical result of Kannan. These results were obtained by designing a surprising new algorithm for the total search problem Range Avoidance: given a circuit mapping n bit strings to n+1 bit strings, find n+1 bit string outside its range. Range Avoidance is a member of the class TFSigma2P of total search problems in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, analogous to its better-known counterpart TFNP in the first level. TFSigma2P was only recently introduced and its structure is not well understood. We investigate here the extent to which algorithms of the kind in recently discovered for Range Avoidance can be applied to other search problems in this class, and prove a variety of results both positive and negative. On the positive side we show that Li's Range Avoidance algorithm can be improved to give a reduction from Range Avoidance to a natural total search problem we call the Linear Ordering Principle or LOP: given a circuit R purportedly defining a total order on n bit strings, find either a witness that R is not a total order or else a minimal element in the ordering. The problem LOP is quite interesting in its own right, as it defines a natural syntactic subclass of S2P which nonetheless maintains most of the interesting properties of S2P; in particular it contains MA and that its exponential analogue requires exponential size circuits. Both of these are consequences of our reduction from Range Avoidance to LOP. On the negative side we prove that the new algorithms developed for Range Avoidance cannot be extended to Strong Range Avoidance, a problem considered in the same paper which first introduced Range Avoidance. In this problem we are given a circuit mapping N-1 elements to N elements, and once again seek a point outside its range. We give a separation in the decision tree (oracle) model showing that this problem cannot be solved with nonadaptive access to a Sigma2P oracle, which in particular rules out all of the new kinds of algorithms recently found for Range Avoidance. This black box separation is derived from a novel depth 3 AC0 circuit lower bound for a total search problem, which we believe is of independent interest from the perspective of circuit complexity: we show that unlike previous depth 3 lower bounds, ours cannot be proven by reduction from a decision problem, and thus requires new techniques specifically tailored to total search problems. Proving lower bounds of this kind was recently proposed by Vyas and Williams in the context of the original (Weak) Avoid problem.
